title: The English Language
description: Ten clear explanations and profiles about English itself: where its words come from, how dictionaries are made, American and British English, spelling, dialects, new words, English as a world language, plain writing, the Bible and the law, and the language of science.

lessons.title: A Dinner Made of Many Languages
lessons.summary: A woman cooks dinner for a friend and looks up where the words on her menu come from.
lessons.text:
Last fall, I invited my friend Nora to dinner, and while I was planning the menu, I became curious about the words on it. A good dictionary gives a short history of each word, usually in small print at the end of the entry. That week, I read those notes, and I found that my simple dinner was a tour of the world.

I started with the garlic. Garlic comes from Old English, the language spoken in England more than a thousand years ago, and it was built from two words: one meaning "spear" and one meaning a plant like an onion. The long, thin leaves of garlic do look a little like spears. The word crab is just as old. People who lived by the sea in England were catching crabs, and calling them crabs, long before French words arrived.

Then I came to the sausage. In 1066, the Normans, who spoke a kind of French, took control of England. The Norman kings were a French-speaking dynasty, and for about three hundred years French was the language of the court and of the rich. Thousands of French words entered English. Sausage came a little later, and it goes back to a Latin word meaning "salted," because salt kept the meat from going bad. Even the word dynasty came to us through French; it began as a Greek word meaning "power."

My dessert was a pumpkin pie, and the word pumpkin has had a long journey. It began as a Greek word for a large melon and reached English through French as pompion. Later, speakers changed the ending, and pompion became pumpkin. I also made a coconut cake. Coconut comes from the speech of Portuguese and Spanish sailors, who called the fruit coco, a word for a grinning face. The three dark spots on a coconut shell look like two eyes and a mouth. English simply added nut.

Nora arrived wearing a piece of red coral on a thin chain. Coral is another traveler: it went from Greek to Latin to French before it reached English. We ate by my window, above a little plaza with a fountain. Plaza is Spanish, and it entered English mainly where Spanish was spoken in America. It comes from a Latin word for a wide street, the same word that gave English the word place.

After dinner, Nora told me that her son had just watched a ninja movie. Ninja is a Japanese word, and it entered everyday English only about 60 years ago. Finally, I put the dishes in a tub of hot water. Tub most likely came from Dutch, brought by traders and sailors in the Middle Ages.

When Nora left, I washed the plates in the tub and thought about the meal once more. English has always borrowed, and it has borrowed from everyone.

Questions:
Which two words from the dinner come from Old English?
Garlic and crab come from Old English.
Why did so many French words enter English after 1066?
The Normans, a French-speaking dynasty, took control of England, and French became the language of the court and the rich.
How did the coconut get its name?
Sailors called it coco, a word for a grinning face, because the three dark spots on its shell look like a face.
Where does the word plaza come from?
Plaza comes from Spanish, and it goes back to a Latin word for a wide street.

lessons.title: How a Dictionary Is Made
lessons.summary: A writer visits a dictionary editor and learns, step by step, how a new entry is written.
lessons.text:
Most of us underestimate the work inside a dictionary. We find a word and close the book, without wondering who wrote the entry or how. Last spring, I spent a day with Ruth Calder, a senior editor at a large American dictionary, and asked her to show me the process.

"The first step is evidence," Ruth said. A dictionary does not invent meanings; it records how people really use words. Her team has a huge database of sentences from books, newspapers, magazines and websites. Before writing an entry, editors read hundreds of real examples of the word.

The second step is deciding which words to include and which to exclude. "People think we choose words we like," Ruth said, "but we exclude words for one reason only: there is not enough evidence." A new word must be used by many different writers, in different places, over several years. A word that was popular for only one summer must wait until it proves that it will last.

The third step is the definition itself, and this, Ruth said, is where a competent editor really shows her skill. A definition must be accurate, short and written in words simpler than the word being defined. It must also capture what a word suggests, not only what it says. Ruth gave me an example. Slim and skinny both describe a thin person, but skinny often carries an implied criticism, the idea that the person is too thin. A competent definition has to show that implied meaning, or the reader may use the word in the wrong situation.

Next comes grammar. The entry tells the reader whether a noun is usually singular or plural, and here the evidence can surprise people. Data was once plural, but today most writers treat it as singular: "the data is clear." The dictionary records both uses, because both are real.

The editors also arrange the senses of a word. Some dictionaries list them by history, showing the progression from the oldest meaning to the newest. Others put the most common meaning first. Either way, the progression of meanings tells a story.

Finally comes checking. Every entry is read by at least two other editors, whose job is to intercept errors before they reach the public. "Our reliability is everything," Ruth told me. "Readers trust us readily, so we must earn that trust." One mistake that is not intercepted can be copied for years, and it can damage the reliability of the whole book.

I asked Ruth how long a single entry takes. "A simple word, an hour," she said. "A word like set, which has hundreds of senses, can take months." I left knowing that I would never underestimate a dictionary again. The small entries I read so readily are the result of careful, patient work.

Questions:
What is the first step in making a dictionary entry?
The first step is evidence: reading hundreds of real examples of the word.
Why does a dictionary exclude some words?
It excludes words when there is not enough evidence that many writers use them over several years.
What implied meaning does the word skinny often have?
It often implies that the person is too thin.
What must a competent definition show?
A competent definition must show what a word suggests, such as an implied criticism.
Why is every entry read by two other editors?
They read it to intercept errors and protect the dictionary's reliability.

lessons.title: Notes from a Semester in London
lessons.summary: An American student in London writes about the small differences between American and British English.
lessons.text:
I am an American college student, and this spring I am spending a semester in London. Before I left, I thought that language would be the one thing I would not have to worry about. After all, the British and I speak the same language. Three weeks later, I am keeping a list of the differences, and it is longer than I expected.

The first difference was on the street. On my first morning, I stepped off the curb and nearly walked into a bus, because I had looked the wrong way. In Britain, people drive on the left, and the steering wheel is on the right side of the car. Kate, my British roommate, told me later that she finds driving in America just as hard, because there the steering wheel is on the left. The curb is different on paper too: the British spell it kerb. The exterior of a car looks the same, but the parts of the exterior have new names: the trunk is the boot, and the hood is the bonnet.

Some words also sound different. Kate says leisure so that the first part rhymes with pleasure, while I say it with a long e, like the word see. Neither of us is wrong. We were talking about leisure and our free time one evening when we realized that we also say tomato differently.

The hardest difference is not in words but in manners. Kate is very polite, and British polite speech is often indirect. When she says that an idea is "quite interesting," she may mean that she does not like it at all. When I showed her my first essay, she said it was "not bad," and I was disappointed. Later, I learned that "not bad" can be real praise. To be polite, the British often say less than they mean, while we often say more.

Kate also uses expressions I have never heard. When I made a joke about her accent, she laughed and said, "Are you taking the mickey?" To take the mickey out of someone means to tease them. She also says that a hard problem is a "sticky wicket." A wicket is part of the game of cricket, and a sticky wicket was once a wet field that made the ball bounce in strange ways. Her grandfather, she told me, still calls nonsense "rot." When he hears a silly opinion, he says, "What rot!"

Of course, words travel in both directions. Crook, meaning a criminal, began as American slang in the nineteenth century, and the British soon borrowed it. Today a crook is a crook in both countries. Kate says that American movies have taught Britain many words, and that British television has taught America just as many.

My list is now four pages long. I still look the wrong way at the curb, but I am getting better. And when Kate calls my work "not bad," I smile, because I know it is polite praise.

Questions:
Why did the student nearly walk into a bus?
The student looked the wrong way, because in Britain people drive on the left.
How do the British spell curb?
They spell it kerb.
What can "not bad" mean in polite British speech?
It can be real praise.
What does it mean to take the mickey out of someone?
It means to tease them.
Where did the word crook, meaning a criminal, begin?
It began as American slang in the nineteenth century.

lessons.title: Why English Spelling Is So Hard
lessons.summary: A teacher explains, with simple examples, where the strange spellings of English come from.
lessons.text:
I have taught English spelling to ten-year-olds for twenty years, and every September I meet the same dread. Children who read beautifully are suddenly afraid of a spelling test. I do not blame them. English spelling is hard, and the dread is reasonable. But I have found that the dread goes away when children learn why spelling is hard, so this is what I tell them.

The first problem is simple math. English has 26 letters, but most accents have about 44 sounds. Some letters must do more than one job, and some sounds must be written in more than one way. Look at dread and breeze. In dread, the letters ea make a short sound, as in bed. In breeze, a different pair of letters, ee, makes a long sound, as in see. And the letters ea can make that long sound too, as in sea. The same sound has several spellings, and the same spelling has several sounds.

The second problem is history. Printing came to England in 1476, and printers began to fix the spelling of words. At that time, however, the pronunciation of English was changing quickly. The spelling stayed where it was, while the sounds moved on. That is why knight has a k: once, people really pronounced it.

The third problem is borrowing. When English takes a word from another language, it often keeps the foreign spelling. Debris came from French, and like many French words, it ends with a letter we do not say. The s in debris is silent. Veil also came from French, and its ei looks strange next to words like sail. Even beautifully hides a piece of French: the eau in it comes from the French word for beautiful. Orphan came from Greek, and like other Greek words, it uses ph for the sound f.

Some words have no vowel letters at all. When the room is loud, I put a finger to my lips and say "Shh!" The children laugh when I write shh on the board, because they can see that it has no a, e, i, o or u.

Luckily, not everything is chaos. English also has patterns, and the patterns can be learned. Take the word bake. When we add -ing, the silent e at the end disappears: baking. When we add -ed, we keep only one e: baked. So we write baking and baked, with no extra e. Another pattern changes y to i: lucky becomes luckily, and happy becomes happily.

At the end of my first lesson, I give a short test with five words: debris, veil, orphan, baking and luckily. By then, the children know the story behind each spelling, and most of them spell all five correctly. The dread, luckily, is gone, and it never comes back as strongly.

Questions:
Why do some children feel dread before a spelling test?
They feel dread because English spelling is hard.
Why does knight have a k?
People once really pronounced the k, and the spelling did not change when the sound did.
Which letter is silent in debris?
The s in debris is silent.
What makes shh an unusual word?
It has no vowel letters at all.
What happens to the silent e in bake when we add -ing?
The silent e disappears, so we write baking; with -ed, we write baked.

lessons.title: The Woman Who Collects Voices
lessons.summary: A profile of a researcher who records the way older people speak in the hills where she grew up.
lessons.text:
Dr. Ellen Hale studies dialects, the different ways a language is spoken in different places. For thirty years, she has driven through the countryside of eastern Kentucky with a recorder, a notebook and plenty of coffee, collecting the voices of older people before their way of speaking disappears.

Her interest began in her hometown, a small town in the hills. Ellen grew up next door to her grandparents, and every grandparent on her street spoke the old mountain speech. Her grandfather called a paper bag a poke and a narrow valley a holler. He said that he was going a-fishing. At school, however, Ellen's teachers told her that this speech was simply wrong. She learned to hide it, and for years she was a little ashamed of her hometown.

At college, she took a class on dialects, and everything changed. Her professor explained that a dialect is not bad English. It is a complete system, with rules of its own. The subject absorbed her completely. She spent whole nights in the library, absorbed in old studies. She discovered, for example, that the a- in a-fishing follows a strict rule. Speakers put it before verbs that end in -ing, but never before nouns that end in -ing. Her grandfather said "a-fishing," but he would never have said "a-building" about a house.

Today, Ellen's work begins with trust. Many older people in the countryside hesitate when a stranger with a recorder knocks on the door. They have been laughed at for the way they talk, and they hesitate to speak freely. So Ellen never hurries. She sits on the porch, drinks the coffee, and asks about family, farming and the old days. She is, above all, a good listener. A good listener, she says, asks short questions and lets the long answers come.

The answers are often wonderful. One farmer told her about the pony he rode to school as a boy, and about the winter the pony carried him home through deep snow. A woman of 94 sang the songs that a grandparent had taught her. People speak most naturally, Ellen has found, when they are talking about things they are fond of, and almost everyone is fond of their childhood.

Ellen has now recorded more than 2,000 hours of speech, which her university keeps for future researchers. What moves her most is the response of the speakers. Many are thankful that someone thinks their speech is worth keeping. One old man, after a long afternoon of stories, held her hand and said he was thankful that his words would live on.

Ellen feels the same gratitude in return. "They give me their time and their memories," she says. "My gratitude is the least I can give back." She still visits her hometown often. And when she is there, she no longer hides the way she talks.

Questions:
What makes a good listener, according to Ellen?
A good listener asks short questions and lets the long answers come.
What did Ellen's teachers say about her grandparents' speech?
They told her that it was simply wrong.
What rule does the a- in a-fishing follow?
Speakers put it before verbs that end in -ing, but never before nouns that end in -ing.
Why do some older people hesitate to talk to Ellen?
They have been laughed at for the way they talk.
Why are many speakers thankful to Ellen?
They are thankful that someone thinks their speech is worth keeping.

lessons.title: How New Words Are Born
lessons.summary: An explanation of the main ways English makes new words, with examples from everyday life.
lessons.text:
English gains hundreds of new words every year. Some disappear quickly, but others stay and soon feel as if they had always been there. Where do they come from? Researchers have found that most new words are made in a few simple ways, and once you know them, you begin to see them everywhere.

The oldest way is to join two words together. This is called compounding. A necklace is a lace, an old word for a cord, that goes around the neck; English speakers first put the two words together more than four hundred years ago. The process still works today. When cameras learned to focus by themselves, the new feature was called autofocus. Autofocus is simply auto, meaning "self," joined to focus.

A second way is blending, in which parts of two words are joined. Pixel is a blend. In 1965, engineers needed a name for the tiny dots that make up a picture on a screen, and they combined pix, a short form of pictures, with el, from element. Today, every photo on your phone is made of millions of pixels.

A third way is clipping, or cutting a long word short. Speakers are busy, and they shorten words they use often. A guitar player plugs into an amp, not an amplifier. Amp is a typical clipping: the first part survived, and the rest was dropped.

New words can also be built on the pattern of old ones. When some people became rich enough to have a thousand million dollars, English already had millionaire, so it was natural to say billionaire. Nobody had to explain billionaire; the pattern did the work.

Sometimes an old word simply takes on a new meaning. A buffer was once a device that softened the blow when two railroad cars hit each other. In computing, a buffer became a place where data waits before it is used, which is why a video sometimes stops to fill its buffer. Lag meant "to fall behind." Today, when a video call freezes, we say the connection has lag.

History, too, creates words. During the First World War, soldiers lived for months in long trenches cut into the ground, and the coats made for them became trench coats. The war ended, but the trench coat stayed in fashion, and so did its name.

Finally, English adds small pieces to the front or back of words. With non-, profit became nonprofit, a word for an organization that does not try to make money. Offshore once described things away from the coast, such as ships or oil platforms. Later, businesses began to move work offshore, to other countries, and a new verb, offshoring, appeared.

None of these methods is new. People were compounding and clipping long before pixels or nonprofits existed. What changes is only the world that the words describe.

Questions:
What is compounding?
Compounding is joining two words together, as in necklace or autofocus.
Which two words were blended to make pixel?
Pix, a short form of pictures, was combined with el, from element.
Why is amp called a clipping?
It is a long word, amplifier, cut short.
What did lag once mean, and what does it mean today?
It meant to fall behind; today it also means a delay in a video call or connection.
How did trench coats get their name?
They were coats made for soldiers who lived in trenches during the First World War.

lessons.title: One Language, Many Owners
lessons.summary: A short report on how English became a world language and how speakers around the world have changed it.
lessons.text:
About 1,500 years ago, English was the language of a few small kingdoms on one island. Today, about 1.5 billion people speak it. Only about a quarter of them learned it as children; the rest learned it at school or at work. How did this happen, and what does it mean for the language?

Part of the answer is power. Britain built a large empire, and in the last century the United States became a world power. Where trade, science and money went, English followed. But power is only part of the story. English also became a practical tool that strangers could share.

Diplomacy is a good example. For about two hundred years, the common language of diplomacy in Europe was French. A diplomat from Russia and a diplomat from Spain would meet and speak French. After the First World War, however, the peace treaty of 1919 was written in both French and English, and English slowly took first place. Today, a young diplomat who cannot work in English will find the job very difficult.

The sky offers another example. Pilots and air traffic controllers around the world transmit their messages in English, so that a Brazilian pilot landing in Japan and a Japanese controller can understand each other. They transmit short, fixed phrases, chosen to be clear even through noise.

Humanitarian work, too, often runs in English. When a humanitarian group sends doctors and engineers from twenty countries to the scene of a flood, English is often the organizational language: the language of meetings, plans and reports. A shared organizational language makes cooperative work possible, and in cooperative projects between many countries, English is the language most people bring.

As English spread, its new speakers changed it. Indian English uses prepone, the opposite of postpone, to mean "move a meeting earlier," a word that standard American English lacks. Australian English gave the world words for its animals, such as joey, a young kangaroo. A joey lives in its mother's pouch for months. Many of the writers who excel in English today grew up in Nigeria, India or Singapore. They excel not by copying London or New York, but by bringing new rhythms and images into the language.

There is a darker side. In some places, English did not simply join local languages; it began to displace them. In Ireland, English slowly displaced Irish as the language of most homes, and many native languages of North America are now spoken by only a few older people. Today, communities and schools are working to keep these languages alive.

English, then, no longer belongs to any one country. In most places it lives beside other languages, and it changes wherever it goes. It belongs to everyone who uses it.

Questions:
Why is English often the organizational language of humanitarian work?
It is the shared language that most people in cooperative projects bring.
What was the common language of diplomacy in Europe before English?
French was the common language of diplomacy.
Why do pilots and controllers transmit their messages in English?
They do it so that people from different countries can understand each other.
What does joey mean in Australian English?
A joey is a young kangaroo.
What happened to Irish in Ireland?
English slowly displaced Irish as the language of most homes.

lessons.title: The Letter Nobody Understood
lessons.summary: A young city employee learns, with his manager's help, how to rewrite a confusing letter in plain English.
lessons.text:
Jamal Owens had worked in the city water office for only a month when his manager, Grace Lin, asked him to write a letter to residents. The city was going to replace old pipes on two hundred streets, and the water would be turned off for one day on each street. Jamal wanted the letter to sound professional, so he wrote it the way he thought official letters should be written.

His first sentence was 62 words long. It mentioned "infrastructure improvement initiatives" and "temporary service delivery changes." It did not say, until the third paragraph, that people would have no water on a certain day. The letter went out on a Monday. By Wednesday, the office phones were ringing with fury. Some residents had not understood that the water would be off. Others thought it would be off for a week. One man said that he had read the letter with disgust. Jamal understood the man's disgust.

Grace stayed calm and showed Jamal a short guide to plain writing. "Here is the proposition," she said. "A letter is written for the reader, not for the writer. The proposition sounds simple, but most of us forget it."

She explained that people who write at work are prone to long words because long words feel safe. Writers are also prone to hiding the main point. "Put the most important fact first," Grace said. "Use the words people use at the kitchen table. If a sentence is longer than 25 words, try cutting it in two."

Jamal admitted that he had tried to make the letter sound slick. Grace shook her head. "Slick language is for selling," she said. "We are not trying to woo anyone. Advertisers woo customers with clever phrases; a city office should simply tell people the facts." She added that confusing letters do real harm. They give the public good reason for anger, and they give the city's critics ammunition. "Every unclear letter is free ammunition for people who say the government does not care."

Jamal felt the sting of rejection, because the letter had been his first big task. But Grace told him that the rejection of a first draft is normal, even for experienced writers, and that the best way to relieve the pressure was to write a better letter quickly.

His second letter began: "Your water will be off on Tuesday, May 14, from 8 in the morning to 5 in the evening, while we replace old pipes on your street." It was short, clear and friendly, and it gave a phone number for questions.

The new letter did much to relieve the residents' worries. The angry calls stopped, and one woman wrote back to thank the office for being clear. Jamal kept her note on his desk.

Questions:
How did residents react to the first letter?
The office phones were ringing with fury, and one man read the letter with disgust.
What proposition did Grace explain to Jamal?
A letter is written for the reader, not for the writer.
Why did Grace say a city office should not use slick language?
Slick language is for selling, and a city office is not trying to woo anyone.
What did Grace say about the rejection of a first draft?
She said that the rejection of a first draft is normal, even for experienced writers.
How did the second letter begin?
It began by saying when the water would be off and why.

lessons.title: The Church, the Court and the English Language
lessons.summary: An explanation of how an old Bible translation and the language of the law left their mark on everyday English.
lessons.text:
Many everyday English phrases come from two places that most people rarely think about: an old translation of the Bible and the language of the courts. Both shaped English for centuries, because people heard their words again and again.

In 1611, a group of about fifty scholars in England finished a new English translation of the Bible, now known as the King James Bible. The translators were experts in theology, the study of religious belief, and in the old languages of the biblical texts, Hebrew and Greek. Every line had to be interpreted carefully, and where the meaning was difficult, it was interpreted by several scholars before they agreed. They also used much of the work of earlier translators, especially William Tyndale.

For the next three hundred years, this translation was read aloud in churches across the English-speaking world. A congregation would hear the same passages every year, from childhood to old age. Each congregation learned the rhythm of the sentences by heart, and many biblical phrases entered ordinary speech. When we call good people "the salt of the earth," or say that we escaped "by the skin of our teeth," we are using biblical phrases, often without knowing it. Excluding Shakespeare, perhaps no single source has given English so many common expressions.

Some words came through the church from much older languages. Amen is a Hebrew word meaning "truly" or "so be it." It passed into Greek and Latin and then into English, where it ends prayers. Today, it is also used outside religion: when a friend says that Friday should be a holiday, you might answer, "Amen to that." Orthodox comes from two Greek words meaning "right" and "opinion." It first described correct belief in theology, but now we speak of an orthodox view in science, art or business, meaning the usual, accepted view.

The courts left their own mark. After the Normans came to England in 1066, French became the language of the law, and English courts used a special legal French for centuries. That is why so many legal words are French: court, judge, jury and crime all came from French. Other legal words came from Latin. Magistrate comes from the Latin word for "master." A magistrate is a judge who handles smaller cases, and in many places a magistrate still decides minor disputes every day.

Legal English also loves pairs, such as "will and testament." Some of these pairs began when lawyers placed an English word, such as will, next to a French or Latin one, such as testament, so that everyone would understand.

The church and the court, then, are two of the great schools of the English language. Excluding a few experts, the people who learned from them never studied language. They simply listened, week after week, until the words became their own.

Questions:
What does orthodox mean outside theology today?
It means the usual, accepted view in a field such as science, art or business.
What is theology?
Theology is the study of religious belief.
How did biblical phrases enter ordinary speech?
A congregation heard the same passages every year, and many phrases entered ordinary speech.
What does amen mean?
It means "truly" or "so be it."
Why are so many legal words French?
After 1066, French became the language of the law in England.

lessons.title: The Greek and Latin Inside Science
lessons.summary: A science teacher shows her students how scientific words are built from old Greek and Latin parts.
lessons.text:
On the first day of her science class, Mrs. Novak writes a list of words on the board and tells her students that they already know more Greek and Latin than they think. Science, she explains, speaks in old words. When scientists need a name for something new, they usually build it from Greek or Latin parts, because those languages were shared by educated people across Europe for centuries. Learn the parts, and the long words become short stories.

She starts with the eye. The optic nerve carries signals from the eye to the brain, and optic comes from a Greek word meaning "of seeing." Then she points to the sky. An eclipse happens when the moon hides the sun, or when the earth's shadow falls on the moon. Eclipse comes from a Greek word meaning "a failing" or "a leaving out": to ancient observers, the sun seemed to fail during an eclipse.

Next come light and sound. In 1800, the astronomer William Herschel discovered invisible light just below red, and it was later called infrared, from the Latin infra, meaning "below." Infrared cameras can see heat, so they can find people in the dark. Sonic comes from the Latin word for sound. When a plane flies faster than sound, it creates a sonic boom, a loud bang heard on the ground.

Then Mrs. Novak holds up a coffee cup. It is ceramic, and ceramic comes from a Greek word for a potter's clay. Engineers now make ceramic parts for engines and spacecraft, but the word still remembers the potter.

Medicine is full of such words. Allergy is surprisingly young: an Austrian doctor made it up in 1906 from two Greek words meaning "other" and "work," because in an allergy the body works in a strange way. Immunity is older. The Latin word immunis described a person who was free from taxes or public duties. Later, doctors borrowed the idea: immunity means being free from a disease. Diagnostic comes from Greek words meaning "to know apart." A diagnostic test helps a doctor tell one illness from another. A nutrient, from the Latin word for "feed," is a substance that feeds the body, and a doctor may test whether a patient is missing an important nutrient.

Mrs. Novak ends with her favorite word, correlation. Its Latin parts mean "a relation together": two things that rise and fall together have a correlation. Ice cream sales and swimming accidents, for example, both increase in summer. "But a correlation," she warns, "is not a cause. Ice cream does not cause accidents. Hot weather causes both."

At the end of the lesson, she asks the class to guess a new word: what might an infrared diagnostic camera do? Most students answer correctly. The Greek and Latin, it seems, are already working.

Questions:
Why do scientists often build new words from Greek or Latin parts?
Those languages were shared by educated people across Europe for centuries.
What does the Latin infra mean?
It means "below."
What is a sonic boom?
It is a loud bang heard on the ground when a plane flies faster than sound.
What did the Latin word immunis describe?
It described a person who was free from taxes or public duties.
Why does a correlation not prove a cause?
Two things can rise together because of a third cause, like hot weather.
